title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral and bold-formatting tokens that begin items in a numbered markdown list (e.g. '4. **', '**6.', '10. **'), rather than on the content of the list item itself. It activates on the structural markup marking the start of a new enumerated point, typically followed by a bolded header phrase, regardless of the topic (budget tips, hobbies, restaurant recommendations, etc.). It is not tied to any particular subject matter or reasoning step, but purely to the recurring syntactic pattern of 'number + period + bold marker' used to delimit list entries. It does not include the full sentence content, prose explanations, or non-list numeric references (e.g. dates, quantities) that lack this list-item formatting.

title: Open-ended clarifying follow-up question
description: This latent fires on conversational, empathetic follow-up questions that invite the user to elaborate further on something they already mentioned, typically phrased as 'Can/Could you tell me more about...' or similar open-ended prompts ('What...', 'Is there...'). The cluster includes therapist- or assistant-style probes seeking additional detail, context, or feelings about a vague referent ('what happened', 'what's going on', 'this person', 'the situation') rather than requesting new factual information or offering advice. It excludes statements, explanations, advice-giving sentences, closed yes/no procedural questions unrelated to elaboration, and declarative reassurances (e.g., 'Sometimes talking about it can help...') that do not themselves solicit further detail from the user. The highest-activating examples are near-verbatim repetitions of the canonical 'Can you tell me more about...' template, while the broader cluster includes semantically similar but more varied elaboration-seeking questions.

title: Validating and contextualizing the user's situation in advice-giving
description: This latent fires on sentences from advice/AITA-style responses that restate the user's (or another party's) situation back to them while framing it as reasonable, understandable, or justified -- e.g. 'it's reasonable to feel frustrated,' 'you were minding your own business,' 'their behavior says more about them than you.' It includes second-person recaps of events ('You were trying to talk to Linda...'), empathetic validations ('it's understandable that...'), and judgments allocating fault or reasonableness between parties in an interpersonal conflict, typically as part of a structured response to a personal-dilemma prompt. It also captures related meta-conversational cues like reading social signals for ending a conversation ('checking their phone,' 'glancing at their watch') that appear in the same advice-column register. It does NOT include purely factual/informational statements unrelated to interpersonal judgment (e.g. adoption cost figures, gaming career lists, archaeology tour descriptions), nor does it include direct instructions or imperatives with no validating/contextualizing framing; the defining feature is the rhetorical act of validating, excusing, or assigning reasonableness/blame regarding someone's actions or feelings, not the topic of the conflict itself.

title: Interpersonal advice-column reasoning
description: This latent fires on sentences from advice/relationship-guidance text (e.g., AITA or Dear Abby style responses) that perform empathetic reasoning about interpersonal conflicts. It captures moves like speculating about another person's unawareness or motives ('She may not be aware of...', 'He might not realize the impact...'), validating the reader's feelings or rights ('You don't owe anyone an explanation', 'It's reasonable to expect...'), and offering hedged behavioral guidance or reframing ('Recognize that...', 'Be cautious and ensure...', idiomatic advice like 'don't put all your eggs in one basket'). It is not simply about any topic involving relationships or money, but specifically the rhetorical stance of a mediating advisor weighing perspectives, excusing/explaining others' behavior, and affirming the reader's boundaries or needs. Sentences that merely state facts, give technical/procedural instructions unrelated to interpersonal judgment (e.g., SSA replacement process, pronunciation guides), or narrate events without this advisory, perspective-taking framing are excluded.

title: Illustrative list of examples (X, Y, or Z)
description: This latent fires on phrases that offer a short list of concrete, interchangeable example options to illustrate a general category, typically phrased as 'This could be A, B, or C' / 'such as A, or B' / a bulleted list of sample suggestions (gifts, activities, chores, small gestures, conversation starters, investment types). The examples are generic, low-stakes, everyday items or activities (a meal, a movie, coffee, chores, a walk) offered as interchangeable illustrations rather than a definitive answer, often following advice-giving or brainstorming ('Examples include...', 'It could be...', 'or "...?"' as a sample question). It also strongly activates on quoted casual small-talk questions/openers ('How was your weekend?', 'Have you tried that new restaurant?') presented as illustrative conversation-starter examples. It does NOT include sentences that make a single definite claim, give a factual/narrative statement without offering alternatives, or state specific personal facts/accusations/arguments (e.g., 'Your roommate offered your beer without asking'), even if they share topical overlap like chores or relationships.

title: Speculative motive-probing in relationship advice
description: This latent fires on advice-style text that speculates about the hidden emotional motives, feelings, or intentions behind another person's (or one's own) behavior in interpersonal/relationship contexts. It includes both direct yes/no or either/or questions posed to the reader ('Is he genuinely interested, or...?', 'Were you defensive or upset?') and declarative hedged explanations offering possible psychological causes ('Perhaps she's had negative experiences...', 'He may not be aware of how his behavior is affecting you'), all centered on interpreting unstated feelings like insecurity, jealousy, fear, guilt, or lack of awareness. It does not include neutral factual statements, advice on concrete actions to take, or general commentary without a speculative 'maybe/perhaps/is it because' framing about someone's inner emotional state. Statements that merely describe events or assert conclusions without hedged speculation or interrogative framing about motive/emotion are excluded.

title: Concluding reminder/advice framing
description: This latent fires on the discourse marker that introduces a summarizing piece of advice, typically at or near the end of an advice-giving response, most often the word 'Remember' (or similar closers like 'Ultimately,' 'Lastly,' 'It's important/essential to remember') used to preface a takeaway about relationships, communication, well-being, or personal growth. The highest-activating examples are dominated by the bare word 'Remember' or short 'Remember that...' fragments, showing the latent tracks the framing device itself rather than the content that follows. The broader cluster includes fuller sentences using this same rhetorical move ('Remember, communication is key', 'Ultimately, it's important to remember that...') as well as closely related hedging/advice-closing phrases ('It's essential to...', 'It's important to recognize that...') that serve the same summarizing-reminder function. It does NOT include ordinary declarative statements of fact, questions, or advice sentences that lack this reminder/summary framing marker -- the key distinguishing feature is the presence of the meta-discourse cue signaling 'here is the key point to take away,' not the specific topic (relationships, ethics, self-care, etc.) being advised on.

title: Empathetic relationship-advice validation
description: This latent fires on sentences from advice/relationship-column style text (e.g., Reddit AITA/advice responses) that validate, interpret, or hedge about someone's emotional experience in an interpersonal conflict. Included sentences typically explain how a person's feelings or reactions 'might have been' caused by another's behavior ('This lack of empathy might have contributed to...'), label an action as hurtful/inconsiderate/unhealthy/understandable, or use stock empathetic openers ('It's understandable that...', 'What a thoughtful question!'). It also captures balanced hedging clauses ('That being said, I do think...', 'However, it's also important to consider...') that soften judgment while still assigning emotional causation or moral evaluation. It does NOT include neutral factual statements, technical/informational content (e.g., car titles, insurance options), or narrative action statements without an evaluative/empathetic framing, even if they appear in the same advice-style texts.

title: Validating/reassuring interpersonal advice statements
description: This latent fires on sentences from advice-column or relationship-counseling style text that validate the reader's feelings, rights, or actions, or gently reframe a situation in emotionally supportive terms (e.g., 'You have every right to feel upset,' 'You're not wrong for feeling hurt,' 'This is not a sign of a healthy relationship'). Included sentences typically use second-person address, affirm autonomy/boundaries, acknowledge emotional complexity ('it's more complicated than that'), or offer reassurance/validation about interpersonal conflicts (family, romantic, social situations). It also captures related hedged reasoning moves like naming a deeper underlying issue or acknowledging counterparty perspectives ('they may be coming from a place of love and concern'). It does NOT include purely factual/technical statements (e.g., explanations of lunar eclipses, cooking tips, banking procedures) even though these appear in the sample, nor does it include neutral narrative description, direct instructions without emotional validation, or first-person disclaimers about AI capability -- the defining feature is the validating, rights-affirming, or perspective-acknowledging rhetorical stance toward a person's feelings or actions in an interpersonal conflict.

description: This latent fires on sentences (often beginning with 'This can/will/could help/lead to...') that state the anticipated benefit, outcome, or consequence of a previously mentioned action or behavior, typically in advice-giving contexts about relationships, emotions, or productivity. title: Empathetic supportive-listening offer
description: This latent fires on formulaic, first-person assistant phrases that offer emotional support, a listening ear, or general help, typically framed as 'I'm here to listen/help/offer support...'. Included sentences are stock empathetic openers or closers used in advice-giving or conversational contexts, such as expressing willingness to listen without judgment, offering to help brainstorm, process feelings, or provide guidance, often ending in an exclamation point or soft qualifier ('if you need it', 'if I can'). It captures the rhetorical gesture of positioning oneself as a supportive, non-judgmental presence rather than any specific content of advice or the topic being discussed. It does NOT include the substantive advice, analysis, or informational content that follows these openers, nor unrelated statements of fact, instructions, or judgments (e.g., 'Verify the letter' or 'By telling her yourself, you can mitigate the harm'), which lack this supportive self-offering framing.

title: Therapeutic validation and reassurance framing
description: This latent fires on sentences in advice/support-style text that validate a person's emotions, decisions, or situation while normalizing them as common, uncontrollable, or process-like ('It's a process', 'Your emotions are valid', 'It's not your fault', 'It's her life and she needs to make her own decisions'). It excludes sentences that merely describe events or actions without an explicit evaluative stance (e.g. narrating what happened), that give advice or recommendations, or that explore possible motivations/causes for behavior without passing judgment on its acceptability.
